item.title: Liberty Leading the People
item.lesson: This is not the Revolution of 1789 — a common mix-up. Delacroix painted the July Revolution of 1830, three days of Paris street fighting that toppled King Charles X, and he painted it within months, hot off the news. The picture's radical move is its hybrid nature: a real, reportorial barricade strewn with real corpses and gunsmoke, led by a woman who is not real at all — Liberty herself, bare-breasted like a classical goddess, tricolor aloft, Phrygian cap on her head. Allegory wades into journalism. Around her, Delacroix assembles all of Paris: a top-hatted bourgeois with a hunting gun (long rumored, wrongly, to be the artist), a street kid waving pistols who helped inspire Victor Hugo's Gavroche, a worker with a saber. The new government bought the painting quickly — then hid it away for most of two decades as too inflammatory to display. Governments have been nervous around it ever since, which is exactly the compliment it deserves.
item.lookFor: Through the smoke on the right, find the towers of Notre-Dame — Delacroix places the fighting in a real, nameable city, then flies a tricolor from the cathedral, a detail contemporaries would have read like a headline.
